paper_title: Learning the 4D World through Point Trajectory Forecasting

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Reliable multi-view forecasting requires videos from different cameras to describe the same evolving 3D scene. To this end, we introduce Video-Point Model (VPM), a world model that conditions on multi-view video histories and a language instruction to jointly forecast future videos from arbitrary viewpoints and the 3D trajectories of persistent scene points. We extend a pretrained world model with camera-conditioned multi-view processing that integrates complementary observations across cameras, and add a trajectory head that predicts how physical points move through time. Each trajectory tracks a single point across all views, and supervising these trajectories alongside video generation therefore anchors appearance changes in every camera to a shared description of 3D motion. To support training and evaluation, we build VPM-Data, a simulation corpus pairing synchronized multi-view videos with persistent point trajectories, and VP-WorldBench, a forecasting benchmark spanning simulated and real environments. We further extend VPM to robot control by adding robot actions as a token modality in the generator. Action tokens share the point-supervised backbone and are denoised jointly with future videos, thereby grounding the policy in the same 3D-aware representation. On VP-WorldBench and existing 4D generation benchmarks, point supervision improves both video fidelity and 3D motion accuracy over a video-only counterpart, and in simulated and real-robot experiments, it also raises the manipulation success of the action-enabled model.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: World models aim to anticipate how scenes evolve from past observations. Recent models pursue this goal by predicting future videos and, for robot interactions, the associated actions (Agarwal et al., 2026). However, visual plausibility alone does not establish whether these forecasts describe coherent 3D motion. Multi-view histories provide richer evidence for predicting this motion by revealing scene structure and ongoing dynamics that may be obscured in individual cameras (Rajiˇc et al., 2025). To exploit this evidence, model must relate observations across cameras to common prediction of scene evolution. Its forecasts from arbitrary viewpoints should therefore depict the same future event, despite differences in perspective and visibility. To connect these predictions, we build on geometric supervision (Lee et al., 2026b) for video modeling, including pointmap prediction and trajectory-derived representation alignment (Liu et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026). Specifically, we investigate jointly forecasting future images and persistent 3D point trajectories. Because each trajectory follows the same scene point over time, it provides common description of motion across cameras. Learning this motion alongside image generation encourages the model to relate appearance changes to the movement of identifiable points. Unlike conventional tracking, both predictions extend beyond the observed history, requiring the model to anticipate correspondences without access to future frames. Our hypothesis is that learning where scene points will move helps the visual predictor produce more faithful forecasts. Accordingly, we introduce VPM, multi-view videopoint world model built on Cosmos 3 (Agarwal et al., 2026). Given posed video histories and language instruction, VPM predicts future videos from arbitrary viewpoints together with the trajectories of points selected from observed frames. To integrate information across cameras, we process their video tokens in shared sequence, using raybased embeddings to encode camera geometry and view axis in positional encoding to distinguish camera streams. trajectory forecasting head is optimized jointly with video generation, allowing explicit point-motion supervision to shape the representation used for visual prediction. To support this learning objective, we construct VPM-Data, simulation corpus covering tabletop manipulation and urban dynamics. Each sequence pairs synchronized multi-view videos with persistent point trajectories, camera geometry, visibility annotations, and language descriptions, providing aligned supervision for future appearance and motion. We complement this training corpus with VP-WorldBench, an evaluation suite spanning simulated and real environments. Its simulation component assesses visual and geometric forecasts on the same held-out events, allowing image quality and motion accuracy to be examined together. We evaluate VPM on our benchmark and existing benchmarks, assessing future-video quality and 3D trajectory accuracy. Controlled ablations demonstrate that point supervision improves visual forecasting. We further investigate whether this benefit extends to robot control through an actionenabled variant that jointly learns video prediction, point trajectories, and robot commands. Across simulated benchmarks and real-robot experiments, point supervision consistently improves task success rates of the action-enabled model. Our contributions are threefold: We introduce VPM, camera-conditioned model that jointly forecasts multi-view videos and persistent 3D point trajectories, using explicit point-motion supervision to improve visual prediction from arbitrary viewpoints. We develop VPM-Data and VP-WorldBench, providing aligned visual and geometric training data and forecasting evaluation suite spanning simulated manipulation, urban dynamics, and real-world recordings. Through extensive experiments and controlled ablations, we demonstrate the benefits of point supervision for multi-view forecasting and assess its contribution to robot action learning in an action-enabled extension.

For multi-view prediction (Balice et al., 2026), SV4D (Xie et al., 2025) synthesizes novel views of observed videos, Geometry-aware 4D Video Generation (Liu et al., 2026) forecasts RGB and pointmaps, and X-WAM (Guo et al., 2026) adds actions to multi-view RGB-D forecasting, while GEM-4D (Zhou et al., 2026b), MECo-WAM (Zhang et al., 2026c), and 4D-WAM (Yang et al., 2026) distill geometry or trajectory fields into video and videoaction representations. Unlike these single-view or per-frame targets, our persistent 3D trajectories retain point identity across views and time. Closest to ours, MVTrack4Gen (Lee et al., 2026b) supervises novel-view generation with multi-view point tracking; we differ from this in that we forecast beyond observed frames, lift supervision from 2D to metric 3D, and extend it to action learning. Video World Models and Action Learning. Video foundation models such as HunyuanVideo1.5 (Wu et al., 2025) and Wan2.2-TI2V-5B (Team et al., 2025) provide pretrained representations for visual prediction. VideoVLA (Shen et al., 2026) and Cosmos 3 (Agarwal et al., 2026) jointly predict future observations and actions, while SpatialVAM (Li et al., 2026b) pairs multi-view RGB prediction with spatial action heatmaps. We instead supervise multi-view forecasting with future 3D point motion and examine whether it also benefits action learning. 3D Motion Forecasting and Benchmarks. Point trackers estimate correspondences within observed videos (Karaev et al., 2025), and TAPIP3D (Zhang et al., 2026a) and MVTracker (Rajiˇc et al., 2025) extend tracking to 3D from monocular and multi-view input. MotionForesight (Bharadhwaj & Jangir, 2026) and MolmoMotion (Zhang et al., 2026b) instead forecast motion beyond observed frames, the latter also supporting video generation and robot learning. Among benchmarks, TAPVidMV (Koppula et al., 2026) provides multi-view tracking annotations and PointMotionBench (Zhang et al., 2026b) targets language-conditioned motion prediction; ours adds paired visual and geometric supervision for jointly evaluating future appearance and point motion.

Tabletop clips replay physics-simulated pick-and-place episodes of Fourier GR-1 T2 robot in Unreal Engine 5, with randomized clutter, surface appearance, scene placement, and camera poses. Distractor interactions are validated and recorded before rendering. Urban clips capture pedestrians and vehicles from running traffic and crowd simulation, varying their appearance, camera intrinsics, and camera paths. In both domains, images and geometric annotations are exported from the same simulation timestep to maintain alignment across views. Annotations and validation. We annotate 256 surface points per object and 512 additional points on the robots arms and hands. Rigid transforms or triangle identities and barycentric coordinates propagate these points through motion and occlusion. Each clip also provides metric depth, camera parameters, point-validity and per-view visibility masks, object visibility states, and visionlanguage-model-generated caption. Clips undergo checks for geometric alignment, annotation completeness, depth validity, camera motion, target visibility, and caption consistency, followed by final human audit. Generation and validation details are provided in Appendix C. 4.2 VP-WORLDBENCH Evaluation splits. The simulation benchmark covers three generalization regimes: 436 new tabletop episodes at varied locations in city C1, whose scenery appears in VPM-Data only as static background; 64 tabletop episodes in two unseen kitchens; and urban clips of moving agents in C1, whose traffic and crowd dynamics are unseen, as urban training uses separate city C2. Each domain includes hard subset in which individual cameras lose sight of the target for at least 30 consecutive frames while at least one camera sees it at every frame. In tabletop hard clips, all three cameras meet this threshold and the target moves while hidden; in urban hard clips, all four cameras lose and re-acquire the target, with two or three meeting the threshold. Details are in Appendix D. Real-world benchmarks. For robot manipulation, we collect 100 teleoperated episodes and sample 3D point tracks on the robot surface from recorded robot states (Appendix B.2). We first evaluate VPM on VP-WorldBench, which covers the same domains as VPM-Data, robot manipulation and general scene dynamics, using held-out episodes and environments along with real-world recordings. Video fidelity metrics are computed for each generated view and averaged across views. We compare two variants: VPM (V), trained only on multi-view videos, and VPM (V+T), our default model, trained on both multi-view videos and 3D point trajectories. Both variants use the same training budget, so the comparison isolates the effect of point supervision. Results. As shown in Table 2, VPM (V+T) achieves the best performance on every split and metric, generating videos with higher fidelity and stronger geometric consistency in both simulated and real-world scenes. Even without point supervision, VPM (V) improves over its Cosmos3-Nano backbone, showing the benefit of multi-view processing. Adding point supervision under the same training budget further improves both fidelity and 3D motion accuracy on all splits, supporting our hypothesis that learning where scene points will move yields more faithful multi-view forecasts. 6.3 ZERO-SHOT 4D GENERATION RESULTS Setup. To assess out-of-domain generalization, we further evaluate on three datasets: ReCamMaster (Bai et al., 2025), CMU Panoptic (Joo et al., 2015), and RoboCasa Kitchen (Nasiriany et al., 2026). Results. As shown in Table 3, VPM (V+T) achieves the best results on both ReCamMaster and CMU Panoptic. We test whether point supervision also benefits robot control using the action-enabled extension of VPM (Section 5). Simulation experiments follow each benchmarks standard protocol with three synchronized views: one wrist camera and one or two third-person cameras on either side of the robot. In the real world, we use the DROID platform (a Franka Research 3 arm with Robotiq 2F-85 gripper) and train only on an 89K-trajectory subset of DROID dataset. We evaluate three pick-and-place tasks of varying difficulty, with 24 trials each. We provide more details in Appendix A.3. Results. As shown in Table 5, VPM (V+T+A) achieves the best success rates on all simulation benchmarks, outperforming both VLA policies and world-action models. This advantage carries over to the real world  (Table 5)  , where VPM (V+T+A) achieves the highest success rate on every task. In both simulated and real-world settings, VPM (V+T+A) consistently improves over VPM (V+A), which is trained without point supervision. These results indicate that forecasting persistent 3D point trajectories provides useful learning signal for robot actions. 6.5 ANALYSIS AND ABLATION STUDIES Modality-wise ablation. We train VPM with combinations of video (V), point trajectories (T), and actions (A). In Table 6, adding trajectories yields the largest gains in video fidelity and 3D motion accuracy on every split, while adding actions yields modest improvements. Training with all three performs best on all splits and metrics, indicating that action supervision complements point supervision. Together with Table 5, where point supervision raises success rates on every benchmark, these results show point trajectories benefit both generation and action. We next examine why. Why 3D point trajectory forecasting helps multi-view video generation. The trajectory head predicts point motion from the generators intermediate features, which the remaining blocks process into future frames, so point supervision directly shapes the representation from which videos are generated. Figure 4 illustrates this coupling: the robot hands and the pedestrian closely follow the predicted trajectories overlaid on the generated frames. Since each trajectory follows single physical point, generation that follows them remains consistent across views. Why 3D point trajectory forecasting helps action prediction. 3D point forecasting supervision consistently improves the action-enabled model  (Table 5)  , which we attribute to three properties. First, on robot data, trajectories are computed from joint states by forward kinematics, describing the same motion as actions but grounded in 3D and in every view, which teaches the backbone to connect visual features with where the robot will move. Second, they are dense, constraining the robots full

Third, object trajectories, where available, specify where manipulated objects should go, encoding the tasks intended outcome. Action tokens, sharing this backbone, thus draw on representation that already encodes the robots future motion. Supporting this, converting predicted trajectories into commands via inverse kinematics, without action tokens, completes unseen real-robot tasks zero-shot (Figure 4). Though not yet consistent enough for quantitative evaluation, these rollouts show that forecast trajectories alone carry actionable information (Appendix A.4).

sections.title: 7 CONCLUSION AND LIMITATIONS
sections.content: We presented VPM, multi-view world model that jointly forecasts future videos and persistent 3D point trajectories from posed video histories and language instructions. With VPM-Data and VPWorldBench, our experiments show that supervising where scene points will move improves visual forecasting on simulated and real benchmarks and carries over to robot action learning. Limitations remain. Our point supervision covers only the robot and annotated objects rather than the full scene; skeletal annotations also omit independent cloth and hair motion. VPM assumes known camera intrinsics and poses at inference, and its cost grows with the number of views, as all camera streams share one token sequence. Future work includes deriving trajectory supervision from real multiview videos at scale, extending it to denser, non-rigid content, and relaxing the need for calibrated cameras.

sections.title: A IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
sections.content: A.1 TRAINING DETAILS We adopt Cosmos3-Nano (Agarwal et al., 2026) as the backbone and follow its Mixture-ofTransformers architecture (Liang et al., 2024). We train VPM with the three-stage pipeline described in Section 3.5. In Stage 1, we train the generation pathway, camera embeddings, and view frequencies with LFM on all multi-view sources, including those without trajectory annotations. In Stage 2, we freeze the remaining parameters and train only the trajectory head and view frequencies with Ltrack. In Stage 3, we jointly optimize the video backbone and the trajectory head with Lforecast. The reasoner is frozen throughout all stages. For video supervision, we treat the camera pose of each view as an optional condition. For instance, views from VPM-Data, where camera control is important, are conditioned on their future camera poses, whereas wrist-camera views from the robot datasets, whose future poses depend on the actions being predicted, are not conditioned on any pose. This also allows VPM to forecast without future camera parameters, as required by our main evaluation protocol. Detailed hyperparameters are provided in Table 7. The trajectory head operates on query and key features from the 18th self-attention layer of the generator and performs = 4 refinement iterations. During training, we sample = 512 query points per clip from the observed history. For the action-enabled variants, we apply Lact in Stage 3 on action-annotated interactions. Following Cosmos 3 (Agarwal et al., 2026), unified actions are represented as 9-dimensional vectors (Zhou et al., 2019). VPM (V) and VPM (V+A) are trained without Ltrack and Lcorr. A.3 ROBOT MANIPULATION TASKS We evaluate all policies on three pick-and-place tasks with Franka Research 3 arm and the DROID camera setup (left and right exterior cameras and wrist camera), as shown in Figure 5. All tasks share tabletop layout with pile of boxes in the middle, and the object and its goal are placed on opposite sides of the pile so that no single camera shows the whole task (Figure 6). The robot puts banana into basket among other fruits, places green cup on plate among cups of other colors, and stacks small blue cube on top of red cube next to green distractor cube, which additionally requires precise placement in height. Solving these tasks requires fusing the three views into consistent 3D understanding of the scene, moving across the pile without touching it, and grounding the instruction among same-category distractors. Each trial is scored as 1 if the object is placed at the goal without touching the pile of boxes, 0.5 if the pick-and-place succeeds but the robot hits the pile on the way, and 0 otherwise. The success rate of task is the average score over its 24 trials, which is why some entries in Table 5 correspond to half-integer counts.

sections.content: To train VPM, we construct 600K samples from three sources: (i) VPM-Data, our multi-view videos with persistent 3D point trajectories from simulation, (ii) robot manipulation video datasets annotated with kinematics-grounded 3D point trajectories, and (iii) open-source video datasets from diverse domains, e.g., MolmoMotion-1M (Zhang et al., 2026b) and Ego-Exo4D (Grauman et al., 2024). We provide detailed statistics in Section B.1, and elaborate on the construction of VPM-Data in Section and robot data in Section B.2, respectively. B.1 DATA STATISTICS We collect 600K samples in total, as summarized in Table 8. VPM-Data contains 10,000 multi-view samples, consisting of 8,000 tabletop manipulation clips and 2,000 urban dynamics clips. The robot datasets contain 91K episodes from DROID (Khazatsky et al., 2024) and HRDexDB (Lim et al., 2026). The remaining clips are collected and sampled from open-source datasets. Our objective is to recover metric, temporally consistent 3D trajectories of action-relevant geometry throughout each manipulation episode. Rather than relying on noisy pseudo-labels from visual point trackers, we construct these trajectories directly from known robot and object geometry together with recorded kinematic states. In particular, robot CAD models provide accurate surface geometry, which can be transformed according to the robot state at each timestep to obtain geometrically grounded 3D point trajectories. We detail this procedure below. 3D Point Extraction. We begin with the CAD or visual meshes of each robot link and manipulated object. We assume calibrated cameras and known transformation between the robot base and each camera coordinate frame. For each mesh, we sample surface points using area-weighted triangle sampling. Sampling is performed once in the mesh-local coordinate system with fixed random seed, and the same points are reused throughout the entire episode. By subsequently transforming these fixed local points according to the corresponding link or object pose at each timestep, we obtain temporally consistent 3D point trajectories without resampling noise. We allocate fixed point budget to each action-relevant component: we sample 256 3D points from the whole robot body. In cases where the 3D points of the target object are available, such as in simulation settings, we also sample 256 points from the object being manipulated. For articulated components composed of multiple meshes, the budget is distributed approximately in proportion to mesh surface area. Let pℓ denote point sampled on the local CAD geometry of link or object ℓ. Because pℓ where (Rw is fixed, point retains the same physical identity over the complete trajectory. For these sampled points, we apply forward kinematics of the robot via saved robot states, and obtain their 3D positions per time step. We replay physics-simulated pick-and-place episodes of Fourier GR-1 T2 robot using recorded joint configurations and object transforms. All distractors avoid the manipulated objects swept volumes. Contact distractors additionally overlap the robots swept volume, with at least 25% of 333 grid inside their bounding box lying within that volume. Urban clips are captured in an open-source driving simulator built on Unreal Engine, using six transformed city tiles with 60 additional building models and fixed noon weather. Vehicles follow the traffic manager and pedestrians follow navigation destinations, amid approximately 30 background vehicles and 40 pedestrians. target is acquired once its instance occupies at least 300 pixels in camera; capture starts after 15 frames of motion. The simulator advances at 1/15 intervals and waits for every sensor before the next tick. Each view contains pixel-aligned RGB, depth, and instance-segmentation sensors, with motion blur and depth of field disabled. Camera configuration. Each camera independently samples its horizontal field of view from 25 to 90. Initial positions are selected from 32 ray-tested azimuths around the target, with distance chosen to control its image coverage. Cameras follow static, arc, translation, random-polyline, or pantilt paths and aim at the target except during scheduled departures. Path control limits translation to 150 cm per frame, changes in the translation step to 20 cm, and rotation to 0.06 times the horizontal field of view per frame. two-stage height filter with 0.5 time constant stabilizes camera aiming without modifying the targets recorded trajectory. D.4 GROUND-TRUTH ANNOTATIONS Persistent points. We sample 256 area-weighted surface points per object once per mesh and preserve their identities across frames and clips. Tabletop points follow recorded rigid transforms. The robot has 512 additional points, divided equally between its arms and allocated across 18 links per side, with at least four points per link and half of each arms budget reserved for the hand and fingers. For urban targets, points store triangle indices, barycentric coordinates, and skinning weights. Per-frame bone transforms recover their positions through linear blend skinning, with rigid components propagated from their attachment transforms. These annotations follow skeletal deformation, not simulated cloth or hair. Coordinates and depth. Stored trajectories use the reference cameras frame at each timestep, in metres under the OpenCV convention (+X right, +Y down, +Z forward). Per-frame 44 world-tocamera matrices and intrinsics are stored for every view, allowing conversion to world coordinates. Motion-based acceptance checks use world-space target motion. Depth is stored as 16-bit PNG in centimetres, with far limits of 200 for kitchens, 650 for tabletop city scenes, and 655 for urban scenes. Visibility labels. For tabletop points projected inside the image, visibility requires camera-space depth + ϵ, where is rendered depth and ϵ = 3 cm. An object is visible when more than 10% of its in-frustum points pass this test; labels also distinguish occlusion, departure from the frustum, and absence. Urban clips contain two target-visibility arrays. visibility uses bounding-box projection and requires at least 300 target-instance pixels for visibility. visibility strict instead uses projected surface points with the same instance-pixel criterion. The bounding-box array supports the visibility acceptance check, while the strict array determines departures, re-acquisition, and hard labels. Language annotations. Each clip receives an English caption from vision-language model. Tabletop captioning uses the recorded object identities, motion, active hand, and scene context; its style checks are advisory. Urban captions are generated from representative video frames after selection, and failing captions are regenerated. All 500 urban captions pass the final style checks. Simulation depth does not reproduce real sensor noise and has invalid sky and out-of-range regions. Camera counts, frame rates, and clip lengths differ by domain. The hard urban subset over-represents pedestrians, and skeletal point annotations omit independent cloth and hair motion. Rendering profiles are fixed rather than calibrated to real camera responses. D.7 REAL-WORLD BENCHMARK DETAILS Real-world human benchmark. Our real-world benchmark split comprises 100 newly recorded 10-second sequences featuring three participants in total. Each sequence includes synchronized multi-view RGB videos, sequence of reconstructed 3D surfaces, and camera parameters. To capture realistic everyday activities, we constructed 23.1 m2 home-like space furnished with sink, cabinets, drawers, refrigerator, sofa, tables, and household objects. Participants move through the space, lift and carry objects, open drawers, and set objects down, producing changes in both human pose and scene configuration. Capture system. We capture RGB videos using 48 FLIR industrial cameras at 30 fps and resolution of 2048 1536 pixels. The camera array combines wide-angle lenses for broad spatial coverage with standard-field-of-view lenses for capturing detail. We synchronize image capture across all cameras using an external hardware trigger. Before recording, we calibrate camera intrinsics using Zhangs method (Zhang, 2000) and estimate extrinsics using 16 calibration boards distributed throughout the room. Specifically, perspective-n-point estimates initialize the relative camera-board poses, which are linked through pose graph in common metric coordinate system. We further refine the calibration through feature matching and bundle adjustment using COLMAP (Schonberger & Frahm, 2016). The calibrated camera parameters are used for image undistortion, 3D reconstruction, and as model inputs. Reconstruction and filtering. We undistort the images using the calibrated camera parameters and reconstruct each timestamp independently with AmbiSuR (Li et al., 2026a), using depth priors from Depth Anything 3 (Lin et al., 2025). For all sequences, we optimize the Gaussians for 2,000 iterations per timestamp before exporting the surfaces. To reduce holes in the reconstructed surfaces, we extract surface points by back-projecting rendered depth maps rather than directly exporting Gaussian as surface points. To reduce floating artifacts, we further filter the reconstructed 3D points. For each point, we count the views in which the rendered depth at its projected image location agrees with its camera-axis depth within 5 mm. We retain only points supported by at least two views and having at least five neighbors within 10 mm radius. Finally, to make downstream tasks computationally tractable, we downsample the filtered points using 1 mm voxel grid, retaining the point with the greatest view support in each occupied voxel.

sections.content: D.8 RELATION TO EXISTING RESOURCES Related resources emphasize complementary annotations and tasks. BEDLAM 2.0 (Tesch et al., 2026) provides human-body geometry, while ReCamMasters Multi-Cam Video dataset (Bai et al., 2025) supports multi-view re-rendering with camera trajectories. TAPVid-MV (Koppula et al., 2026) evaluates multi-view point tracking, and PointMotionBench (Zhang et al., 2026b) evaluates language-conditioned point-motion forecasting. Our simulation benchmark pairs future multi-view appearance with metric surface-point trajectories, camera geometry, depth, visibility, and language on the same clips.

F.6 ABLATION STUDY FOR TRAINING DATA Setup. Our training data combines three sources  (Table 8)  : VPM-Data (10K samples), robot manipulation datasets with kinematics-grounded point tracks (91K), and open-source videos (504K). We train VPM (V+T) while leaving out one source at time and report the change in FVD and δ3D avg with respect to the model trained on all sources in Figure 10. Results. Each source mainly benefits the evaluation domain it covers. Removing VPM-Data causes the largest degradation on the simulation splits, especially on Simulation General (+48.3% FVD and 9.16 δ3D avg), since it is the only source that pairs synchronized multi-view urban videos with persistent 3D trajectories. Removing VPM-Data also lowers δ3D avg on Real-world General by 3.31, suggesting that its accurate simulated trajectories transfer to real human motion. Removing the robot datasets mainly affects Real-world Robot (+18.2% FVD and 12.39 δ3D avg), and removing the open-source videos mainly affects Real-world General (+12.2% FVD and 6.73 δ3D avg). Removing any source degrades every split, indicating that the three sources are complementary.
